title: Who is a Jew?
hookLine: Orthodox and Conservative follow the mother's line; Reform and Reconstructionist also accept the father's, with upbringing

cards: Two cousins at a family wedding. Both grew up with Shabbat dinners at their grandmother's, both learned Hebrew, both had a bar or bat mitzvah. One cousin's mother is Jewish.
The other cousin's father is Jewish, and his mother is not. At the reception someone asks, half joking, which of them the synagogue across town would count as Jewish. The table goes quiet.
The honest reply is: it depends on which synagogue. You heard the short version on day forty-five. Today, the fuller one.

teach.b: Who is a Jew? The classic rule comes first.

The Mishnah, in the tractate on marriage, teaches that when a Jewish father and a mother who is not Jewish have a child, the child follows the mother. The Talmud reads this out of a verse in Deuteronomy.
In rabbinic law, then, Jewish status passes through the mother, and a person can also become Jewish by conversion, which is tomorrow's story. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism keep this rule.
Now a surprise inside the rule: some things still pass through the father.
In the Torah, the people are counted "after their families, by the house of their fathers," and to this day a kohen, a member of the priestly family, is a kohen because his father was.
So even in traditional law, the mother's line and the father's line each carry something. Then the other answer.
Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism also accept a child of a Jewish father, when the child is raised as a Jew and takes part in Jewish life.
For them, a Jewish parent on either side opens the door, and the upbringing walks through it.
And for real people: the two cousins may be welcomed in one synagogue and asked about their mother in another.
Each stream is trying to be faithful to what it holds, and none needs to be painted as cruel or careless to explain itself.
Different answers, given with conviction, and real families living right across the line between them.

how: Orthodox and Conservative communities count as Jewish a child of a Jewish mother or a convert; Reform and Reconstructionist communities also count a child of a Jewish father who is raised with Jewish identity and practice.

games.q: what does “who is a jew?” mean?
o: a riddle children ask at the Passover seder
a status question the movements answer in different ways
a test every Jew must pass before a bar mitzvah

games.q: who is a Jew? — tap the pairs.

s: in traditional law, nothing passes through the father
a kohen is a kohen because his father was.
Reform Judaism accepts a child of a Jewish father who is raised as a Jew
every stream gives the same answer
the streams give different answers, held with conviction.

games.q: you're the cousin whose father is Jewish and mother is not. you were raised with Shabbat and Hebrew. how do the streams count you?
o: every stream counts you as Jewish.
Reform and Reconstructionist count you; Orthodox and Conservative look to the mother's line.
games.why: Reform and Reconstructionist accept a Jewish father with a Jewish upbringing; Orthodox and Conservative follow the mother's line, with conversion as the other door.

practice: Choose a family you know, maybe your own, with more than one tradition or more than one answer in it: a cousin, a stepchild, a friend whose parents came from two worlds.
Notice that the question of who they are lands on them, not on a committee. Wish them well, in whatever words are yours, then let the picture rest.

wordCard.voice: Who is a Jew? Orthodox and Conservative Judaism follow the mother's line; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism also accept the father's, with a Jewish upbringing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: different answers. On this path, there's still no test at the door. See you tomorrow.
